sections.text: Every value in Rust has a type. Scalar types hold a single value: integers, floating-point numbers, booleans and characters.
Integers come in signed (i8, i16, i32, i64, i128) and unsigned (u8 up to u128) sizes. i32 is the default. usize is used for counts and indexes.
Rust usually works out the type for you. Add `: Type` after the name when you want to be explicit, or when Rust can't guess.
Floats are f64 (the default) and f32. bool is true or false. char is a single Unicode character in single quotes:
Dividing two integers drops the remainder, so 7 / 2 is 3. Use floats when you need the fraction.

Rust never converts between number types on its own. To mix them, convert with `as`: `let total = items as f64 * price;`. If an integer overflows in a debug build, the program stops with an error instead of silently wrapping.
The _ in 1_250 is just for readability, like a comma in 1,250.

exercise.prompt: Convert count to f64 with as so the program can compute the average. It should print: 2.5
